617.title: Har Rai and Har Krishan
617.hook: remember Guru Har Rai, and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes
617.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and take water from its sarovar for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday: miri piri, and your line: arjan, hargobind. Today the Ardas names the seventh Guru, and the eighth, who was a child.

In the middle of New Delhi, a short walk from the government buildings, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool of water. Every day, people carry the water home in bottles: for a sick parent, for a child with a fever, for themselves. Ask why, and you'll hear about a boy. Tradition says a deadly epidemic, remembered as smallpox, was moving through Delhi, and a Guru who was still a child stayed in the city and went among the sick. That place is Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, and the boy is remembered every time the Ardas is said.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `WATER CARRIED HOME IN BOTTLES.` → `A GURU WHO WAS A CHILD.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line runs on: sri harirai, remember the revered Har Rai. Then: sri harkrishan dhiaaeeai, jis ditthai sabh dukh jaai. Meditate on Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes. Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, was the grandson of Guru Hargobind. He is remembered for his gentleness. Tradition says he kept a garden and a dispensary of herbal medicines at Kiratpur, open to anyone who needed them, and a well-known story says that once, when his robe brushed a flower and broke it, he was saddened, and spoke about how easily we damage what we can't mend. His son, Har Krishan, became Guru while still a small child. He was called to Delhi, and while he was there, the epidemic broke out. Tradition says he tended the sick in the city, and that he caught the disease himself and died there, still a child. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands where he stayed. Look at what the Ardas says. It doesn't call him small, or young, or tragic. It says: seeing him, all pain goes. Dukh, the Punjabi word for pain and sorrow, simply leaves. People who have sat with a sick relative sometimes describe what happens when a small child walks into the room: the air changes. The Ardas sets that ordinary experience at the heart of the prayer: a child's calm face, and the pain going out of a room. A gentle father, then his child, a Guru who stayed when it was dangerous.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child you know, or once knew, or once were, at a quiet moment, asleep or absorbed in a game, and let their face stay in front of you. Let some of today's tension go out on the breath, the way it goes out of a room when a child walks in. If you pray, say Waheguru, or the Ardas's own words, sabh dukh jaai, all pain goes.
Dukh, pain or sorrow. Seeing Guru Har Krishan, the child Guru who stayed among the sick, all dukh goes.
Your line: all pain goes. A child who stayed when it was dangerous. See you tomorrow.

618.title: The nine treasures
618.hook: remember Guru Tegh Bahadur and the nine treasures come running home
618.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs say that remembering Guru Tegh Bahadur brings the nine treasures running home, and Gurbani often names the Name of God as the true nine treasures.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukh, and your line: all pain goes. Today the Ardas reaches the ninth Guru, the one we spent a month with.

There's a strange thing in this line of the Ardas, and once you see it, it's hard to unsee. For a month we read Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks: the world is a dream, nothing stays, strength gone, all companions gone. And we know how his life ended: arrested, imprisoned, executed in Delhi. By any ordinary measure, he lost everything the world can take. Yet when the Ardas reaches his name, it promises the opposite of loss. Remember him, it says, and every kind of treasure comes running to your house. How does the man who lost everything become the one who brings everything home?
screen: `A MONTH OF NOTHING STAYS.` → `HE LOST EVERYTHING THE WORLD TAKES.` → `AND THE ARDAS PROMISES TREASURE.`

segments.voice: The line is: tegh bahaadar simariai, ghar nau nidh aavai dhaai. Remember Tegh Bahadur, and the nine treasures come running home. Nau is nine. Nidh is a treasure, a store of wealth. In old Indian lore, the nine treasures belonged to the god of riches: nine kinds of fabulous wealth, everything a person could want. In ordinary use, nau nidh can stand for every good thing at once. And notice the verb: aavai dhaai, comes running. Runs, like a child to the door. The Sukhmani Sahib, for one, says the nine treasures are the Name of God: whoever has the Name lacks nothing. So the promise in the Ardas works on two levels. On the plain level, Sikhs ask that remembering the ninth Guru bring blessing to their homes. On the deeper level, it echoes his own saloks. The last one said: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The man who lost everything the world can take was holding the one treasure it can't. Remember his name, too. He was born Tyag Mal; tradition says he was given the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword, after fighting bravely as a young man beside his father, Guru Hargobind. Brave of the sword, and yet remembered for the treasure he held in his heart. That's the paradox the Ardas sets in one line: the poorest-looking moment, and the richest.
screen: `NAU NIDH: THE NINE TREASURES.` · `AAVAI DHAAI: THEY COME RUNNING.` · `THE REAL TREASURE IS THE NAME.` · `TYAG MAL, BRAVE OF THE SWORD.` · then, large: `NINE TREASURES HOME.`

segments.voice: Picture your home, or a home you love, and fill it slowly, not with money but with the treasures that would actually make it rich: a laugh at the dinner table, someone who listens, a quiet morning, a faith or a hope, a friend who drops by. Name each one as it arrives, and notice which are already there. If you pray, say Waheguru, as the one treasure Gurbani says holds the rest.
Nau nidh, the nine treasures. Every good thing, and in Gurbani, the Name; remember the ninth Guru, and they come running home.
Your line: nine treasures home. The richest things in a house were never bought. Day six hundred eighteen, done.

619.title: Help everywhere
619.hook: Guru Gobind Singh, be our help everywhere
619.howItsDone: After remembering the first nine Gurus in Guru Gobind Singh's own stanza, the Ardas names the tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, and asks him to be the community's help in every place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nau nidh, the nine treasures, and your line: nine treasures home. Today, the tenth Guru, and the last line of the opening stanza.

Here's a detail that's easy to miss when the Ardas goes by at full speed. Guru Gobind Singh wrote its opening stanza. He names Guru Nanak, then each Guru after him, one by one, all the way to his own father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. And then he stops. Of course he doesn't name himself: it's his poem. But Sikhs who pray the Ardas today hear the tenth Guru's name right after the ninth, in exactly the same words. Someone added it, and the words they chose had been sitting at the end of the stanza all along.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU WROTE THE STANZA.` → `HE STOPS AT HIS FATHER.` → `SOMEONE ADDED HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The stanza ends: sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, be our help in every place. Sabh is all. Thaaeen is places. Sahaai, an old friend by now, is the helper. So the Var's opening asks every Guru it has named to be our help, everywhere. Then the Ardas, as Sikhs pray it, goes on: dasvaan paatshaah, sri guru gobind singh sahib ji, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai. The tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, be our help in every place. The community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet. The one who left himself out is written back in. And it fits him. He became Guru as a boy, after his father's execution. He wrote poetry and, tradition says, kept a court of poets at Anandpur. He founded the Khalsa. He fought battles, lost his sons, and lived through siege, flight and grief. And before his death, Sikh tradition says, he ended the line of human Gurus: from then on the Guru would be the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa community. So this isn't a vague wish. It's asked of someone remembered in the court and on the battlefield, in the forest and in grief. Sikhs ask him to be present wherever they go: the job interview, the hospital waiting room, the long drive home. And the prayer doesn't ask for help in some places. Sabh thaaeen. All of them.
screen: `SABH THAAEEN: IN EVERY PLACE.` · `THE POEM'S LINE, GIVEN TO THE POET.` · `A LIFE THAT WENT EVERYWHERE.` · `ALL PLACES, NOT SOME.` · then, large: `HELP EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Think of the places you'll be this week, your desk, your car, a hard conversation, your own kitchen late at night, and pick the one where you feel most alone. Picture yourself there. If you pray, ask in the Ardas's own words, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, and feel that it includes this place; if you don't, picture someone you trust standing beside you.

620.title: The light of the ten
620.hook: the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib, the embodied light of the ten Gurus
620.tomorrow: The five, the four, the forty
620.howItsDone: After naming the ten Gurus, the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib as the light of the ten masters, and the sangat answers Waheguru aloud; Sikhs bow before it and treat it as the living Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: help everywhere, and your line: present in every place. The Ardas has now named all ten Gurus. Today it turns to the one in front of the room.

At a candlelight vigil, the first candle is lit with a match. After that, nobody uses a match again. Each person tips their wick into the flame of the person next to them, and the light moves down the line. By the end there are hundreds of candles, but in a sense only ever one flame, passed along. Sikhs have used an image very like this for more than four hundred years, for how the Guruship moved from Guru Nanak to the next Guru, and the next. And the Ardas, having named all ten, now says where that flame is today.
screen: `ONE MATCH, THEN NO MORE.` → `WICK TO FLAME, DOWN THE LINE.` → `HUNDREDS OF CANDLES, ONE FLAME.`

segments.voice: After the tenth Guru, the Ardas goes on: dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot, sri guru granth sahib ji. The light of the ten masters, the Guru Granth Sahib. Jot is light, a flame, the kind that burns in a lamp. In paraphrase, the line continues: fixing your mind on its reading and the sight of it, say Waheguru! And here, for the first time in the Ardas, the whole room answers aloud: Waheguru. The idea of one light passing on is old. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the bards Satta and Balwand sang that when Guru Nanak installed Guru Angad, it was the same light and the same way; only the body changed. Sikhs understand each Guru as carrying the one jot in a new body, ten times. Then in 1708, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship not to a person but to the scripture. The flame that went from candle to candle now burns in a book. That's why Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book about the Guru, but as the Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Someone waves a chaur, a whisk, over it as it's read. At night it's carried to its own room to rest. People bow when they come into its presence. From outside, that can look like honoring an object. Sikhs would say it's honoring a presence: the light of all ten, in one place, still speaking.
screen: `JOT: THE LIGHT IN THE LAMP.` · `SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `THE FLAME NOW BURNS IN A BOOK.` · `HONORING A PRESENCE.` · then, large: `THE TEN IN ONE.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a page of the Granth, in a gurdwara or on a screen; if not, picture it: the Gurmukhi letters in long lines, the cloth around it, the canopy above. Let your eyes rest on the page the way they'd rest on a candle flame, without trying to read it all. If you pray, say Waheguru, the room's answer, once, quietly.

621.title: The five, the four, the forty
621.hook: it remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty liberated
621.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty Muktas in one line; five initiated Sikhs still lead every amrit ceremony, and the Sahibzade's martyrdom is marked each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jot, and your line: the ten in one, the light of ten Gurus in the Granth. Now the Ardas turns from the Gurus to the Sikhs who stood with them.

Three numbers. Say them fast and they sound like a phone number: five, four, forty. Each one is a group of people. One group stepped forward when everyone else stepped back. One was four brothers, two of them still small boys. One walked away from their Guru, and then came back. The Ardas says all three numbers in a single breath, right after the Guru Granth Sahib, before any other Sikhs it remembers.
screen: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.` → `THREE GROUPS OF PEOPLE.` → `SAID IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The line goes: panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan. The five beloved, the four princes, the forty liberated. The five are the Panj Pyare. At Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Sikh tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh stood before a huge gathering with a sword and asked for someone willing to give their head. A long silence. Then one man stood. Then four more. As the story is told, they came from different castes and regions: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water carrier, a washerman, a barber. They were the first initiated into the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him. Ever since, five initiated Sikhs lead the amrit ceremony. The four are the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. The older two, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting at Chamkaur. The younger two, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, still small boys, were captured and executed at Sirhind after, tradition says, refusing to give up their faith. Sikhs mark their martyrdom every year. The forty are the Chali Mukte. During the siege of Anandpur, a group of Sikhs left the Guru and, tradition says, signed a paper disowning him. At home they were shamed for it, and a woman named Mai Bhago led them back. They fought at Khidrana, now Muktsar, and fell. As the last of them lay dying, the story goes, the Guru tore up the paper. That's why they're called mukte, the liberated. Five who stepped forward, four who held on, forty who came back: Sikhs hear in them three ways a person can be faithful.
screen: `THE FIVE: WHO STOOD UP.` · `THE FOUR: THE GURU'S SONS.` · `THE FORTY: WHO CAME BACK.` · `THREE WAYS TO BE FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.`

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say five, and picture people standing up in a silent crowd; on the next, four, and picture four brothers, two grown and two small; on the next, forty, people walking back toward someone they'd left. Repeat it slowly, and notice which you understand best right now: stepping forward, holding on, or coming back. If you pray, follow with Waheguru.
The five. The Panj Pyare who stood up, the four Sahibzade, and the forty who came back: remembered in one breath.
Your line: five, four, forty. Three numbers, three groups, said in one breath. That's day six hundred twenty-one.

622.hook: the steadfast, those who meditated, shared food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword
622.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the steadfast, those who meditated, shared their food, ran the langar and wielded the sword; vand chhakna, sharing, is counted among the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five, and your line: five, four, forty, three groups in one breath. Today the Ardas widens out to people with no names at all.

In a gurdwara kitchen somewhere, a woman has been on her feet since five in the morning, rolling more rotis than anyone could count. Nobody knows her full name; the kids just call her auntie ji. She'll never be in a history book. Out front, a man has swept the same gurdwara steps every Sunday for thirty years. The Ardas, having remembered the five, the four and the forty, now remembers people like them: not by name, but by what they did with their hands and their days. It's a list of verbs.
screen: `AUNTIE JI, SINCE FIVE A.M.` → `THE MAN WHO SWEEPS THE STEPS.` → `REMEMBERED BY WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: Listen to the run of it: hathiaan, japiaan, tapiaan. The hathi are the steadfast, who held firm and wouldn't be moved off their faith. The japi kept the Name and the banis going, day after day. The tapi lived with discipline and endured hardship. Then, what they did: jinhaan naam japiaa, who meditated on the Name. Vand chhakiaa, who shared what they had, and then ate. Deg chalaaee, who kept the cooking pot going, who ran the langar. Tegh vaahee, who wielded the sword to protect others. Vand chhakiaa is one of what Sikhs often call the three pillars: naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing. Sikh teachers like to point to the order: vand, then chhak. Share, then eat, not eat and share the leftovers. The kitchen and the sword sit side by side, too. Deg and tegh: feeding and protecting, named together as two halves of looking after people. Those two words come back later in the Ardas. Then the line names what these people left behind: their kamaaee, a word for earnings, what you earn by labor. The Ardas asks the room to fix its mind on the kamaaee of these beloved, truthful ones. Not their fame. Their earnings, built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning. So every time Sikhs pray, people like auntie ji are remembered, even if nobody there knows her name.
screen: `HATHI, JAPI, TAPI: THE STEADFAST.` · `VAND CHHAKIAA: SHARE, THEN EAT.` · `THE POT AND THE SWORD, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `KAMAAEE: WHAT THEY EARNED.` · then, large: `THE SHARERS.`

segments.voice: Think through today's meals and pick one you could share: a little extra for a neighbor, an extra place at the table, or simply serving someone else first. Picture yourself doing it, share first, then eat, and notice how small the act is, and how old. If you pray, say Waheguru as you decide.
Kamaaee, earnings built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning. Hathi, japi, tapi; those who shared, then ate, kept the pot going and held the sword: remembered for their kamaaee.
Your line: the sharers. First the sharing, then the meal, and nobody needs to know. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 622 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THOSE WHO SAW AND OVERLOOKED.`

623.title: Those who saw and overlooked
623.hook: those who saw others' faults and chose to overlook them
623.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who saw others' faults and overlooked them, dekh ke andith keetaa, alongside the steadfast and those who shared, served and protected.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamaaee, earnings built up quietly, and your line: the sharers. Today, the last verb in that same list.

Your roommate leaves the dishes again. A coworker takes credit for something you did. Your brother says the thing he always says at family dinners. You see it. You absolutely see it. And then there's a fork in the road, a split second where you decide what to do with what you saw. The path there is well worn: file it away, bring it up later, tell someone else. The Ardas, in its list of people Sikhs remember with honor, includes one group whose only deed is what they did at that fork.
screen: `THE DISHES, AGAIN.` → `YOU SEE IT.` → `A FORK IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Right after those who shared their food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword, the Ardas adds: dekh ke andith keetaa. Dekh ke: having seen. Andith: unseen. Keetaa: made it. Having seen, they made it unseen. It doesn't say they didn't notice. They weren't naive. They saw clearly, and then chose to treat it as if they hadn't. Sikhs hear it first about other people's faults and the wrongs done to them: they saw, and let it go. Some also hear it about temptation: they saw what could have pulled them off course, and looked away. Gurbani has the same spirit elsewhere. Among the saloks of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib, one says, in paraphrase: do good even to the one who does you harm, and don't let anger settle in your mind. Now, a balance. The very same line honors those who wielded the sword. So overlooking isn't pretending injustice doesn't exist, or refusing to protect people. A Sikh is asked to stand up against cruelty. Andith is about something smaller and more daily: the slights, the irritations, the faults of the people around you that you could keep score of, and don't. A family, a friendship, a shared kitchen: each runs partly on people who quietly decided not to mention it. The Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast. Their deed was invisible on purpose. That's the point.
screen: `DEKH KE: HAVING SEEN.` · `ANDITH KEETAA: THEY MADE IT UNSEEN.` · `FARID: DO GOOD TO THE ONE WHO HARMS.` · `NOT INJUSTICE: THE DAILY SLIGHTS.` · then, large: `SEE, AND OVERLOOK.`

segments.voice: Let one small irritation come to mind, something someone does that you keep noticing; not a real wrong that needs facing, just something small. See it clearly, once, then picture yourself setting it down, the way you'd put a pebble from your shoe back on the path. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set it down.
Andith, unseen. Dekh ke andith keetaa: having seen clearly, they chose to make it unseen.
Your line: see, and overlook. Seeing clearly comes first, and letting go comes second. Day six hundred twenty-three, done.

chat.says: 'Having seen, they made it unseen.' So the Ardas praises people who ignore injustice?
options: No: they saw clearly and let small slights go. The same line honors those who protected others.
Yes: it teaches that a Sikh should never respond to any wrong, however serious it is.
No: it means they never noticed anyone's faults at all, because they weren't looking.
chat.meaning: Dekh ke andith keetaa: they saw clearly, then chose to let it go. Overlooking daily slights isn't ignoring cruelty; the same line honors the sword.
